utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Radic, before we start again, I would like to remind that you you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'd like to begin where we left off yesterday concerning the conversations that you had at the beginning of August 1995, after Operation Storm. And we talked yesterday about the understanding that there was going to be -- according to Ambassador Galbraith, 80 per cent of the Serbs would not come back. Now let us direct our attention back to these transcripts and focus on some of the conversations that you had. And the first one that I'd like to deal with is P463, which is the conversation between you and President Tudjman on the 22nd of August. And if I could turn our attention to page 10 in the English and page 9 in -- excuse me. Page 9 in the B/C/S. Now, I want to talk to you about the centre of that page, and given the fact that I do not read B/C/S, I ask whether or not that's on the page. Beginning with: "Okay, I'm talking about 10 per cent ..."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not in the B/C/S version on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it should be page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Page 14 of the B/C/S, then. Thank you, Counsel. That does not appear to be it either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in this -- in the paragraph you say: "Okay, I'm talking about 10 per cent. So the first priority of colonising is this right here, in my opinion, Petrova and Zrinski Gore. That's where we have to establish some kind of a city sooner or later." Beginning in the next paragraph. You say: "However by our companies, opening factories, just as the Serbs did in Licki Osijek. I visited that factory. That looks marvellous." If we can turn two pages further on, in page 12 in the English where the president begins: "Listen, I am meeting with the army tomorrow." He notes: "The army is a priority, followed by development" -- that's page 18 in the B/C/S. Next page in the B/C/S. That's it, okay, fine. He notes that: "The army is a priority, followed by development, because with the army we begin at once." And I believe overnight you were handed the Exhibit P464 which is a transcript of the conversation with the military leaders that took place the next day. Now in the sequence of these conversations we're talking about opening factories, building cities, having the military move in there to develop the area. And I would like to ask you a question based on the cross-examination by the Prosecutor, if the point of all this activity is just to keep the Serbs out and from returning, if that's the point, why are you insisting on doing all this development in these areas?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely the goal was not for the Serbs to keep them out. The only real goal here was for this region, which was underpopulated, very sparsely populated, to settle it. And on several occasions here, we said that we should move in the army as well, as I said, we thought it was better to move the members of the army here, rather than in already existing large towns. And also, we wanted to initiate some factories. We already had some factories in a somewhat more southern region in, Licki Osijek, but over there, there were a couple of hundreds of apartments that were owned by the state and that were empty at the time, so the main goal was to bring people back there. And we started from the fact that -- from our assumption, that many of the Serbs that left would not come back. So this is why we wanted to incentivise the Croats, to move there and this is why we later on adopted the Law on the Areas of Special State Concern. That region per se is not particularly attractive. Without additional incentives, people would not move there. This is why we thought we needed to incentivise them to settle there. And the first and the easiest activity was obviously to go there with the army, with the army which would settle there, because the members of the army have their wives and children, and the wife's could work in a textile factory over there; children could start their schooling there. So this means that the life in this region would be initiated. So this was our strategic goal, our strategic task at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. I would like to shift gears with you and talk to you a little bit about some of the questions that were put to with regard to your conversation again with President Tudjman concerning Mr. Pasic. And again we are back at P463, the conversation on 22 August. And if we could turn to page 6 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S. And this is the conversation that took place with you and the President where you discuss Mr. Pasic being a Serb. Now, you recall, and you know about the law on ethnic minorities, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I can recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on the Law of Ethnic minorities, in an ethnically Serb city based on the 1991 census, you would have to have an ethnically Serb mayor, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole point of this story was that in the areas from which people moved out, there were more or less two mayors. One of them was a Serb who lived in Knin, for example, if we take Knin then as an example, and the Serbs of -- citizens of Knin chose him, elected him for their mayor. And the other one was elected by people who moved out from Knin, but very often this election was impossible to organise and this is why the government appointed that person. So from the minimal number of people, because you know that during the time when Knin was occupied there were very few Serbs from Knin who lived away from Knin, and from them we had to choose somebody, to elect him a mayor. And this is why I told the President that we have somebody who is incompetent, and then I'm also reminding him that is he a Serb, just to remind him that we had to select somebody as a mayor based on the Law on Ethnic minorities, one of the Serbs, not out of the ranks of competent people, but out of the ranks of a particular ethnicity. So now that we were about to start with reconstruction, my opinion was that this person who maybe was capable to carry out some administrative work while being displaced he is incompetent to initiate all these works, all the reconstruction, the very difficult task that was now ahead, and this is why I thought that possibly we now to select somebody else. So my point here was not his ethnicity but, rather, my doubt whether he was a capable of carrying out such a serious task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The point, Mr. Radic, is, is that the reason why you are talking about the ethnicity of the mayor is because the Law on Ethnic Minorities requires you and the President to consider the ethnicity of that mayor; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. That was the law at the time, according to which the mayor of Knin had to be a Serb. And in some other municipalities of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this Law on Ethnic Minorities --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I am referring, Mr. President, we don't need to go through that whole matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of the Law of Minorities, and I think we have dealt with that and also in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. And if I can refer the Chamber - and I won't need to go into this - to P639 where Ms. Rehn who testified here described the law as the adoption of -- this is on page 6, paragraph 11, the adoption of this law was considered to be one of the essential conditions of the international recognition of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in this context when President Tudjman says, Change this individual, because the Croats are now a minority in Knin -- excuse me. The Croats are now a majority, my apologies, and he is concerned about the competence of this individual. Is that the essence of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. So the emphasise here was on the competences and not on ethnicity, and this was my point of view, and I'm convinced that this was the President's point of view as well. But this was a colloquial conversation, so we did not give any precise descriptions. At that time I did not have to remind the president, You know, Mr. President, pursuant to the law on ethnic minorities we have to do this or that, but with this fact that I said that he was a Serb, I simply reminded him that this had to do with the Law on Ethnic Minorities which was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I have been informed that if we could just keep our pace down a little bit, Mr. Radic, I think the translators would be very happy with that. This Chamber has received evidence that Mr. Pasic, notwithstanding President Tudjman's desire to change that, Mr. Pasic stayed in position in Knin until March of 1996. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I know that, because of that, we had some technical problems. Knin could not function well enough. It would have been better to have somebody who was operationally more competent and more experienced with the matters of economics, for example. Maybe I can add here, that, in 1996, one of the most competent people we had was appointed the mayor of Knin. Prior to that he was mayor of Split, the second largest town of Croatia. This was Mr. Pujic, and once he came to Knin, the whole life in Knin was organised completely differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. I'd like to shift gears just a bit and talk to you a bit about the status of the Serbs who left the Krajina after Operation Storm. And yesterday we talked in -- of the situation in Western Slavonia of the Serbs after being asked to leave -- excuse me, asked to say, left. My apologies. And now we want to move what happened just prior to Operation Storm and the aftermath, when the Serbs in fact left. And let's just take this step by step. And if we can, I'd like to talk to you at the beginning of Operation Storm. Just prior to that, the VONS meeting that you attended on 3 August 1995, and if we could bring that up in D1454. And if we could just go to the cover page. Mr. Radic, you can see in the first line of the people present at the meeting, you were present at that meeting. And do you recall this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Possibly the best memory of any meetings I have ever participated in is from this one, because, at that meeting, we said we would start with liberation of our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you're saying you will start with liberation of the country what you're saying is that the government decided to commence with Operation Storm at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it in the following way. This was a decision of President Tudjman as commander in-chief, and he informed us his closest leadership, at this meeting about his decision, and we all supported his decision. So you could say that this was a key meeting and the decision was that the next morning we would start liberating the occupied territories of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the one part of this meeting that I'd like to talk to you about is the comments by President Tudjman on giving some information to the Serbs and making an announcement to the Serbs in the Krajina to stay. Now we talked yesterday about how such an announcement was made in Western Slavonia for the Serbs to say. And I would like to turn our attention to page 22 of 32 in the English, and page 43 in the B/C/S. And we'll go towards the bottom of the page in English, and beginning with the "dobro" in B/C/S. Do you see that, Mr. Radic, in the middle of the page the president says: "Very well. Let's get to work. I haven't heard the opinion on this. I said I thought we should address the Serb population. We would call the Serbs to lay down their weapons. At the same time we could say that we would vouch for their civil rights, and after that, the implementation of the elections in the spirit of ... law and so forth. We would also tell the international communities [sic] that the Serbs do not accept a peaceful solution." "So, do you think that it would be sufficient to address only the Serbs? I have to sign that appeal to them." And there is an interruption where somebody says: "Only to the Serbs, for now." Now, Mr. Radic, you know, do you not, that in fact the next day, the President did make a public appeal to the Serb population to stay, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Already in the morning hours, all the Croatian media that could be heard in the occupied territory admitted this message by President to the Serbs, that they should stay, that nothing would happen to them and that they should stay as an element of the Croatian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me refer to D1809. And I believe it's page -- the part is page 2 in the English, beginning with "I invite the members of the Serbian paramilitary forces," and page 2 in the B/C/S. Thank you. Just up little further.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the section that says -- the paragraph beginning: "I invite the members of the Serbian paramilitary forces who are voluntarily or forcefully [sic] mobilised in the Serbian paramilitary forces to surrender their weapons to Croatian authority, with the guarantee that they will be given amnesty, according to the valid Croatian laws. "I invite the instigators of the rebellion to understand the futility of their undertaking and its damage to the Serbian community in Croatia if they persist in this rebellion, to surrender to Croatian authorities and accept the pardon or legal trial for their offences. "I invite the Croatian citizens of Serbian nationality, which have not actively partaken in the rebellion to stay at their homes, and without fear for their life or property, welcome the Croatian authorities with assurances that they will be given all civil rights and will be enabled elections for local administration according to the Croatian constitution and constitutional law with the presence of international observers."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the evidence before this Chamber is that any number of witnesses have heard this and have testified about it. In order, it is Sava Mirkovic, P723, paragraph 3; protected Witness 54, P-- at P186, page 3; another witness, Petar Kolovic, testified to this at P631, paragraph 3; Stepan Zaric, Exhibit P2516, paragraph 3; Mile Sovilj, P86, paragraph 9, and so forth. Others have testified, and certainly we will not [sic] provide at the pertinent time the individuals who have all testified to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, asking the Serbs to stay and the decision by those Serbs to leave, voluntarily leave, was a significant event for the Republic of Croatia and how they had -- were going do deal with those people; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly. At this meeting that you have referred to, and at many others prior to this one, the definite position was what the President wrote here, that many Serbs had been misled, that they had taken part in the rebellion without knowing where this was going take them, and the president and all of us on a number of occasions said loud and clear, Stay, nothing will happen to you. But something happened contrary to the will of the President. They left of their own free will. It wasn't the Croatian politics or the Croatian Army who had chased them away. Someone else had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, it's a fact that they not only left of their own free will, but they joined a force with which the Republic of Croatia was at war. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I ask for some foundation for the claim that all the Serbs that left joined a force that was at war? I'm not sure that is well founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll clarify the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the people that left voluntarily, voluntarily went to another country, to stay in another country, or countries, both of which were at war with the Republic of Croatia. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, or at least for me, personally, it is difficult for me to imagine that a person would voluntarily leave his home, and that is why my conclusion is that this was an organised process, that the greater Serbian authorities had made these plans much earlier and had encouraged and organised the Serbs together with the withdrawal of the armed forces for the Serbs to leave with them. I wasn't there, but my deep conviction is that they were forced, in a sense, to leave by what Milosevic is synonymous for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers that you're not staying well within the boundaries the Chamber has set for cross-examination. Would you therefore please get back into those boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was covering exactly what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you to go back into those boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, now, with the idea these individuals who left and how they were going to be treated, these people who left were not citizens of the Republic of Croatia, were they?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, they were not citizens of the Republic of Croatia. They only had the right to file a request for Croatian nationality, because they were born in Croatia. Those who had born in Croatia were entitled to apply for Croatian citizenship. And that was one of the basis of the rebellion. They didn't wish to be Croatian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, without going through this, the Chamber has heard the exhibits, and I'm not going to go through this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But again, we don't have to list them all in the presence of the witness. The Chamber is, perhaps not in every detail and page number, but is aware of the evidence which is before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And likewise, Mr. Radic, you know that these individuals in the Republic of Serb Krajina or the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina said that they were in fact citizens of the Republic of Serb Krajina and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then changed to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is common knowledge. Not only did they claim that they were citizens of the republic of Yugoslavia, but they even claimed that they would attach this part of Croatia to Yugoslavia. That was the aim and the basis of the rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarification. You said those who were born in Croatia that they had the right to apply for Croatian citizenship between in the intermediate period -- well, the situation was quite different. What was the percentage of persons who, well, let's say, in July 1995, lived in Croatia and were of Serbian ethnicity? What was the percentage that was born this Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard for me to tell and to give you the figure off the bat. But shall we say, about 60-odd per cent who had been born in Croatia and some 40-odd were people who had come from other parts of the former Yugoslavia, from Bosnia, from Serbia, and other areas, and who were living in Croatia and working there. This applied mostly to the Yugoslav Army, the police and many other spheres of activity. But that is my impression. I can't give you the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now with regard to these individuals, just to summarize, Mr. Radic, the Republic of Croatia did not consider the people that left the Serb Krajina to be Croatian citizens and those individuals, Serbs from the Serb Krajina, did not consider themselves to be Croatian citizens. Is that not accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fact. But the President, in this letter too, called on those who wanted to be Croatian citizens to stay, to accept the facts. Now it was up to their will or due to somebody forcing them to make such a decision to decide what they decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you heard, did you not, President Tudjman refer to those people who left as people who opted out of being a citizen of the Republic of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened during the period that followed, when we saw that they had left, yes, the President repeated this several times. I must also say that he knew better than many of us others this segment of the population because he had lived for a considerable part of his life in Belgrade. President Tudjman was a general of the Yugoslav Army and he spent a large part of his life in Belgrade, and he was far more familiar with the way people thought there than those who were younger than he.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, Ambassador Galbraith told this Chamber, and this is at P444 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the focus of the Chamber in its examination-in-chief clearly was to further explore what was said in meetings which this witness attended. We are now going through the whole of the policy of President Tudjman on which we had heard already quite a lot of evidence. That is not, and I repeat therefore, that the Chamber really would like to you go back to the boundaries that were set by the Chamber, since you have asked no permission to do otherwise, and it was clearly in our guidance, so therefore, again, unanimously the Chamber considers that you're not staying within the boundaries set. Could you please now really get back --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, and what I was attempting to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm saying, but you are always explaining what you are attempting to do. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have just one second to explain the contextualisation of all of these conversations, which I submit to the Chamber is missing, and that is, number one, that people didn't think they were coming back; and, number two, the concept was of -- of President Tudjman, when we go into Galbraith and what Galbraith said, which the Chamber brought up, was simply this. Excuse me, Mr. President, let me finish. It is simply this: That President Tudjman was of the belief that they didn't have these rights because they opted out and joined a warring force. That gives contextualisation to everything that the Chamber asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you could -- Mr. Kehoe, in this concept of yours you could go through the whole of the evidence again as contextualisation of what the Chamber was focussing on, and clearly that is not what the Chamber expected to you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Ms. Gustafson did the same thing, and there was no complaint by the Chamber when Ms. Gustafson did the same thing. I am attempting to allow to give as much information to the Chamber as possible as to the mindset of one of the participants to this meeting with another participant who is dead as to how they are coming into this meeting. One, they don't think they're coming back; and, two, they don't think they have a right to come back, which, of course, explains in large part the difference of opinion between Ambassador Galbraith and the participants of this conversation. Because if you go back to the exhibit offered by the Prosecution, Galbraith's testimony and his statement at P444, paragraph 33, he is talking precisely about this which is -- which is Tudjman saying these people opted out. It is a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the testimony of Mr. Galbraith, as you, yourself, pointed out very clearly was specifically focussed on a certain meeting with -- with the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that is not accurate. If you go back to Galbraith's statement he is not talking about a particular meeting; he is talking about a sequence of meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The element that was touched upon, the Chamber has a feeling, has gained the impression that are you further away. I let you go earlier as well. It is not to say that not one step outside of those meetings is allowed, but you are moving further away from what was the focus of the Chamber than Ms. Gustafson did. And I asked you to get in -- back into the boundaries. And if you put one step over those boundaries, I would not have intervened, but it is the unanimous impression of this Chamber that we are already with two feet out of the boundaries. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, of course I object, and at the appropriate time, I would like to put my objections on the record more elaborately than I have to date simply because I think this is an extremely important consideration if the Chamber is going to put any credence on these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, again, let us talk about the contextualisation of these conversations of moving people in, of what exactly, and we're talking about 426, the Law on the Temporary Takeover that you on 11th of August, we're talking about the conversation with President Tudjman in P463 on 22nd of August, 1995 where you are talking about building factories and cities. I'm talking about the conversation in P464, the next day with the military, talking about putting the military in to generate this area. Now, this is all being done, of course, in the context of the Republic of Croatia still being at war. And given the fact that they are at war, it was still a major security concern in the development of these areas. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the time, the war was at its peak and the deployment of our military units was certainly strategically aimed at defence, due to the fact that Milosevic was still in power. He had still not been overthrown. And army had to be where it was important for the defence of Croatia. And in this context, if this is positive in the demographic, economic, and every other sense, then it is essential that several parameters form a positive whole. The fact is that the area is empty, abandoned, and for every house to be preserved regardless of who used to have to lived in it, it was important to settle people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that score I direct the attention to the stipulation of the Gotovina Defence to the pre-trial brief filed by the Prosecution, and I'm referring of course to paragraphs 105, 106, and 107, where, inter alia, the Prosecution maintained that an armed conflict existed between the HV and the RSK through -- including and not limited to the end of the operative time of the indictment and also that the -- that Croatia and Serbia, more broadly, was likewise in an armed conflict during this operative time-frame. So suffice it to say for this entire period of time the Republic of Croatia was in armed conflict with a combined Serbs forces. Now, based on that, based on the fact that there was still a war there was, nevertheless, members of the international community, including Ambassador Galbraith, who wanted, notwithstanding the war, wanted a mass return of Serbs who had left; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that Galbraith talked about mass return, at least not when I was present. He may have said that in any of his public addresses. But what I recall much better is that we always talked about it, that realistically a smaller number of people who left Croatia was going to return. Personally, I did not have any personal -- or friendly relationships with Mr. Galbraith, so I did not meet with him very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to a video that has previously come into evidence in this case with an announcement by Minister Granic. It is Exhibit 1821 which discusses the public position of Croatia with regard to mass returns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, Dr. Mate Granic, received today the representatives of the EU; the French ambassador to Zagreb, Jean-Jacques Gaillarde; and" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the interpreters have not received, as they report, transcripts of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's verify that. Are the transcript available or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have a transcript from 28th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm now moving to the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth has a transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transcripts are there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why don't we just start this from the beginning if we can. Okay. If we may play this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is 28 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] The deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, Dr. Mate Granic, received today the representatives of the EU, the French ambassador Zagreb Jean-Jacques Gaillarde, and first secretaries of the Spanish and Italian Embassies, Camilo Villarino Marzo and Benedetto Laterri, at their own request, and also present at the meeting was the representative of the European Commission with the European Union Monitoring Mission, Fulvio Paolini. The representatives of the countries of the European Trojka expressed the EU's concern to Mr. Granic regarding the situation involving human rights in the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia, emphasising that Croatia strongly condemns all incidents in those areas. Minister Granic said that these were individual incidents which before all show the level of frustration people have, and expressed his belief that with the stablisation of civilian authorities, the reasons for concern over the situation regarding human rights will no longer exist. With respect to the return of refugee Serbs from the liberated areas, Minister Granic pointed out that their return will unavoidably depend on the possibilities of achieving a final peaceful solution of the crisis in these areas and the normalisation of relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In present circumstances, individual requests will be received and processed in accordance with the Croatian laws."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the position with regard to the return of Serbs was -- that would depend on the normalisation of relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia except, of course, humanitarian concerns might dictate that individuals would be brought back. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this was the -- not only the public position, this was the position that was talked about privately and talked about among the ministers that there were as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was a public fact, but this was also something that we talked about on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radic, that in fact did happen, that after the normalisation of relations with the Federal republic of Yugoslavia, then the organised return of people from, be it, the Bosnia-Herzegovina or from Serbia began to come back into the area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It has happened to a large extent, but after the war, after the refugees were exchanged, after we collected information on the victims of the war, the casualties, and all the rest, it was possible to organise to organise the return. And yesterday we already saw the information that President Tudjman, in Vukovar several years later, said that 14.500 people came back. So as the normalisation progressed, so the possibilities to have an organised return were also larger. At the same time, the reconstruction was ongoing and we had more technical preconditions which allowed for people to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And those technical preconditions I think you talked to us previously was an application and receipt of Croatian citizenship and then an application for return; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us now shift gears again, and I want to go back into some of the conversation that we had the early part of August that have to do with -- and I'm talking about your private conversations that are taking place and policies that were discussed privately as well as publicly. And first I'd like to highlight your concerns and the first document that -- and I recognise there are a series of meetings here, but one of them is on the 7th of August, 1995, D813. D1813, excuse me. And this is a -- in fact, this is an open session meeting on the 7th of August. And if we could go to page 30 in the English. And this is a series of people speaking, Mr. Radic, Mr. Valentic -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could have page 26 in e-court and 59 -- excuse me. 20 in English and 45 in B/C/S. In e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, I would like to discuss with you both the conversations that you were having publicly as well as the conversations you were having privately, about problems in the area, especially right after Operation Storm. And it's paragraph that I would like to highlight and it's a long discussion by you. This -- well, it doesn't have you on this particular page. Trust me, this is you speaking. And in this paragraph, where it begins: "There are just one or two very important things I have to stress ..." Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All right. "So there are just one or two very important things I have to stress. Activities for the return of people cannot evolve spontaneously. It has to be organised very precisely and very well. So from this, the [sic] government, we are not now sending an invitation to returnees to rush back ... we shall call you, we shall organise those [sic] things, and say tomorrow, or on this or that day, we shall return to Drnis, Vrlika, or whatever area necessary, in an organised fashion." Now I take it from that, that you were very concerned about people just rushing back into this area without any semblance of order. Now tell us why.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day before I made this speech at the government meeting I was informed that a returnee had been killed in Lovinac. It was a Croatian village that had been completely destroyed during the war in the area between Gradac and Gospic, and our citizen returnee between Gracac, therefore -- and Gospic, and when he was removing the branches to enter his home, he was killed by a mine. And under the influence of that event to avoid there being a hundred, maybe thousand such incidents, we said that we have to carefully organise these things. We could not allow the returnees to rush back to their villages on their own. It was necessary to renew the infrastructure, to clear the roads, to re-establish the electricity grid, the water supply, and then village by village, small town by small town, starting from the places where it was less dangerous and easier to organise to bring back the people. It would be ideal if everything had been in place that nothing had been mined or destroyed. We could have said, Come back tomorrow. But as it is, without any documentation, this was not possible. And that is why, at the very beginning, we appealed on people to wait to be invited back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you also talked to us in -- in the examination over the past several days about people coming back, and the transcript themselves talk about people coming back. And destruction ensued. And in your private conversations with the President, and let me direct your attention again to P463, page 4 of 37, and page 6 in the B/C/S where you talk about that. Now, as this is coming up, Mr. Radic, part of your job in assessing bringing people back is a determination of a level of damage to various areas and what your office is going to have to do to fix those premises so people can be brought back from hotels on the coast or wherever they happened to be. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We organised the return, or the renewal of the returning process, so that the first two steps were de-mining and assessment of the damage. So larger expert teams went into the field to make an estimate of the damage so that we could organise our next steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the bottom of this page, and we'll talk about another issue where you begin at: "However..." Should be the bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just turn the page in the B/C/S to 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note: "However, one thing I have to tell you is that I visited all of this now both by car and by helicopter. Our men torched a lot, they were [sic] torching today, as they did yesterday, Mr. President [sic], it's no good."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in English. Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "I went to Kijevo to see, I know that area very well. There's a village Civljane near Kijevo, of equal size, a Serb village where they renewed nice houses and told them everything has been preserved. I got there on the day of the assumption of the Virgin Mary to find everything had been burned down."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Not in the cities because the authorities were obviously more powerfully there, but in the villages. It's not the army, it's that 5th echelon which is under I don't know whose what kind of banner, put on a uniform, warned about, those are the worst tramps, torching and looting around. That is our property; it is not someone else's. What if he burned down the Serb village near Kijevo where we could accommodate our population? Here, I received a letter of the same content from the cardinal asking me and saying that he had received a letter from some Cilko guy saying that our men are torching those places over there. I'm not telling you hearsay, but the things that I've experienced myself and seen with my own eyes, torching and looting." If we could turn to page 7 in the English, at the top of the page in English, the carry-over sentence is you speaking. And page 10 in the B/C/S. The top of the page, it's you continuing to speak to President Tudjman: "But there transitional period is a period of robbing, misery, and all kinds of things. I do not see a way to prevent all this" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm told we don't have the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have that page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I will get it forthwith. Should be page 10 of the B/C/S at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably page 9. Probably 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe it is starting there at the bottom, Mr. Radic. This is the comment: "There's a period of robbing, misery, and call kinds of things." Turn the page in the B/C/S. "I do not see a way to prevent all this, but the worst evil is to torch and destroy" --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have the page in Croatian. I think it is the previous page, page 9 in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree, sorry. It's page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we just go one page back please in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, each page -- e-court numbers are one ahead of the hard copy page numbering. If you keep that in mind, it may be easier to direct the witness to the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe we are at the centre of this page here, sir. And it notes in that sentences, again: "This is the transition period, there's a period of robbing, misery, and all kinds of things. I do not see a way to prevent all this. But the worse evil is to torch and destroy." There's a comment by the President. And if we can go to the next page in the B/C/S. And the President after your comment says: "We talked about preventing this from the beginning." Now, we are talking about what you're saying privately to the President and also what you're saying publicly, and we'll get into the public. Talk to us about this discussion, talk to us about your level of frustration in this particular private conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that this issue arises from the -- relates to the topics that the Chamber covered in direct examination not does it arise out of the Prosecutions cross-examination. And if the Chamber decides to allow this area to be covered, I will need some time to recross-examine thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe in your e-mail to us or your Chamber staff e-mail to us, you refer to issues of a security concerns and conversations in both a private and a public setting. Certainly this issue, albeit not specifically addressed by the Chamber, does fall into the category of security concerns and both the private and public nature of those conversations with, once again, a participant to this conversation with the President of the Republic of Croatia, who is obviously dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, security concerns, but perhaps there's a misunderstanding, was -- the Chamber was talking primarily about security concerns as we found it in the area north and south of Karlovac where Croatia was cut off and how issues of colonisation, as it was called now, and then how that would address security concerns, and that was also the focus. You may remember that we had a -- quite a number of questions in relation to the 10 per cent where we wanted to know exactly where it was and what the concerns were, and how the population of the area would meet some concerns of -- this balanced composition of the population. That's the kind of security concerns we had in mind at the time. And I think, also, which was shown in our examination-in-chief to be part of our focus. I do not remember that in the examination-in-chief there -- the question of whether one was opposed against burning and looting or not, that that was addressed, either in the examination -- as a focal point. It was, if at all, it was a marginal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I have to say that I was somewhat surprised that the Chamber did not address this for the simple reason that I understood the purpose in part, of course, of calling this witness was to examine the intent of the Croatian authorities or members of the JCE prior to and going through Operation Storm. Now, certainly this individual and his activities concerning the temporary -- the Law on the Temporary Takeover, et cetera, played into that. This particular comment on this, given that it is part and parcel of the JCE as charged by the Office of the Prosecutor in paragraph 12, goes directly to the burning or destruction or devastation aspects that the -- that the OTP has levelled in this regard. Now, I did note that the Chamber did talk about some destruction concerning Donji Lapac, but -- excuse me, the OTP did. And -- and certainly it plays into that. But, more broadly, Mr. President, this particular evidence directly goes to the JCE which I do believe the Chamber is very concerned with, and given that, we have the unique opportunity to talk to an individual who was in these conversations and to talk about what was going on during the circle of these conversations. So, again, I thought that the Chamber was going to re-cover that. I thought that, given the nature of this evidence, going to the intent aspect prior to Operation Storm, it was important to ascertain the intent element on these other issues, such as burning, because that has been a central feature of the intent element from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're invited to move on to another subject. The Chamber will during the break further consider where exactly to draw the lines. That means that there may be or may not be an opportunity to further explore this matter after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, of course, if the Chamber would like any further elaboration on exhibits or the path I was intending to travel upon, I would likewise do that before the break as well. Should I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving away from this topic for one moment, Mr. Radic, and I'd like to certainly begin a discussion on the Law of the Temporary Takeover that was raised both by the Chamber and certainly by the Office of the Prosecutor. And again, once again I ask you to keep in mind the time sequence that we are discussing here, beginning with this conversation on the 11th, where the issue raised is, What are we going to do with all this property? If we talk at the beginning -- and it has been discussed at some length, P462.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to let you know, Mr. Radic, what I'd like to take you through is the evolution of this decree and statute and the ultimate discussions as they progressed, if I may. So if we get some idea of exactly where I'm going I would like to give you a preview of that and, of course, this is it the first discussion we have on this score. And there's a debate going on, and I think that the Chamber has highlighted some aspects of it. I believe that they -- if you turn to page 10 of this document in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't believe that's page -- excuse me. Take us to page 15 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now we begin a discussion about the law itself and some of the practical concerns about the law of people moving in and out. And there's a discussion by Mr. Valentic, where, if someone moves in and someone else comes back, they'll have to move and minister Susak says: "No one [sic] will move in under such a law." Mr. Radic, when you're discussing the implementation of this law, there's some very practical problems about moving people in and moving people out and reconstruction and what happens after the house is reconstructed, and what happens if someone comes back. And isn't that a reality, the practical concern of moving population in and out of these houses?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. This was the period immediately after the Operation Storm. The war is still going on, a time when many homes are completely or partially destroyed, when there is the danger of some being further destroyed, when many looters are roaming around, stealing property from those homes, we don't have the strength to prevent all that in the villages, so there is a host of practical issues which are not just of a legislative nature, and these are things that had to be seriously discussed at the time. And at meetings, people presented various ideas, but then in a smaller group, a smaller team at the government, we agreed on a draft law which was discussed and adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us just talk a little bit about the various discussions that are taking place, and even on this page -- excuse me. If we can scroll down to Mr. Krpina's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read it to you in English because I think we can get the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 24 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krpina says: "Mr. President, I think we should pass a law, that they would declare all -- that they would declare all abandoned property state law [sic] on the pretext of preserving the property." He talks about it being a pretext. And that there were other conversations. If we go to, for instance, page 22 in the English -- excuse me, page 20 in the English where Mr. Sarinic is talking about how property was -- of the French was dealt with in Algeria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the page before that in English, and 28 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. Sarinic is talking about, in the centre of that comment: "I asked about the case when the French left Algeria?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page in the English, the comments by Mr. Milas in the centre of the page, and the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas talks about: "The Czech constitutional court has recently confirmed the decree from 1945 on the simple appropriation of property, the decree by Benes, the president of the republic, and the constitutional court confirmed that it is legal and it is still in effect. They haven't made much progress ..." So the discussion is in many different areas, including the Benes decrees, which appropriated, in 1945, property of the ethnic German population. Early on we're talking about a wide variety of proposals on how to deal with all this vacant property, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting, there were people with considerable international experience. Mr. Sarinic had spent his life in France. Mr. Milas in Austria and Czechoslovakia, and they conveyed the experiences other countries had in similar cases, and all this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us move to the actual continued discussion as we move closer to the implementation date at the end of August and the beginning of September, and I'd like to direct you to a transcript that was read in part by the Chamber, and that was D1823, which is a closed session of the government of the 31st of August, 1995. I want you to keep in mind as this is coming up, Mr. Radic, that we have a sequence of ideas going on from early -- the early August on pretexts or appropriation of property, and I want to direct you to exactly the conversation that is taking place here that is directed, in large part, by the prime minister, Mr. Valentic. Now, if we could turn to page 2 of 30 in the English, and I will tell you, Mr. Radic, that even though there's not a cover sheet on this that lists all the participants, you are speaking in this document at some length, so I just want to advise you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it begins with the paragraph: "As you may have seen." And we're talking about this potential decree on the Law on the Temporary Takeover, and I'd like to read you a sequence of items. This is Mr. Valentic, Prime Minister Valentic speaking: "As you may have seen, it is actually about the necessity to protect the property which, de facto, lost its proprietor, the property worth billions; the property which is under no one's protection, and which is, largely because of that, partly burned and robbed. Unless this property is not placed under protection, it is practically impossible to protect this property in this large area. We are fully aware of the possible political implications, and that is why we opted for the solution that we deem have to have factual, political, and legal justification. That is why I would like to ask Vice-President Misetic to elaborate on this law and this decree; maybe I should explain why we decided to come up with this decree."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to talk you through the discussion by Mr. Misetic concerning the people who left the Krajina. And that is the third category that begins in the centre of the -- in the centre of the English page -- yes, towards the bottom of the -- that's the paragraph in B/C/S. "The third category is the property of those citizens, primarily of those in the occupied territories who left the Republic of Croatia after the liberation of those occupied territories; all ... three categories of property are rated by this law as a property without the proprietor as their proprietors left the Republic of Croatia. The purpose of this is law to make this property subject to proper management in the way the good governor would do so [sic] in order to avoid an unfathomable damage to this property, as well as to ensure that, although

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: property, a number of Croatian citizens [sic] primarily the Croats who are expelled by the Serbs from other areas and from other countries would benefit from this property." Continuing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, if we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Bearing in mind the fact that up until now, and from now on, every single Croatian move on the international level shall be scrutinised from the point of view of international humanitarian law as well as the fact that the Croatian state has becoming a military and political factor, and a factor in general, not only in the territories of the former Yugoslavia but also in Europe and in the world, taking up the role of political subject in these areas, there have been quite a few proposals an opinions. The final proposal of the co-ordinating bodies for internal affairs and of all others who took part in creation of this law is that all this property is to be sequestered by the Croatian state, meaning that the state of Croatia shall be responsible for its management, rather than to state in a law or in an enactment that this is property of the Republic of Croatia." Now, I notice we're at break time, Mr. Radic, I would like to discuss this meeting with you at some length. It is going take a little bit of time, Mr. President, and I do believe it will take us well past the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask the usher to escort Mr. Radic out of the courtroom. We will have a break, Mr. Radic, so that I can further inquire with the parties about the time still needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started yesterday. We are now one session. Could you give us a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the most an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think so, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As matters stand now, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions in view of Mr. Kehoe's questioning, Your Honour. I don't need any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also not in view of the Chamber's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will only have ten minutes questioning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Then we will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber has considered the scope of cross-examination. If you would like to put a few focussed questions, in relation to the minutes, where looting and burning appears, although the Chamber has not directly addressed that matter as one of the real subjects of its examination, then you're allowed to do so. At the same time, the Chamber expects you not to go through the whole looting and burning issue again, then focussed on those portions of the transcript. Therefore -- Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if that is Your Honour's ruling, you know, I just would like to draw Your Honours attention that this was witness was on the witness list of the Gotovina Defence. This is hardly the unique opportunity that Mr. Kehoe referred to earlier, and I would like to add that if this topic is going to be raised for the first time in cross-examination, and even if is a few questions, it relates to a relatively central issue in this case, I will need time to prepare, and I will need time to re-cross-examine this witness on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's first wait and see what the questions of Mr. Kehoe are. Mr. Kehoe, what Ms. Gustafson said is that if this matter would be raised first with this witness -- the Chamber already addressed that matter, to some extent in its communication with the parties, that the parties decided not to call this witness, and you could have done that if you would have wished to do so, and, therefore, there are limitations. Let's really try to see whether we can focus not on the looting and burning as such. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, I will, of course, if need be, address the concerns of the OTP, if Your Honour wants to; but if not, I'll just move ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, before we go back to the looting and burning issues, let's just stay with what we left off with, which was the temporary takeover law. And we just read both comments by both Mr. Valentic and also comments by Mr. Misetic, and if I could just address you to one last entry in D1863, and I'm talking about page 28 in the English and 46 in the B/C/S. And in the paragraph where Prime Minister Valentic talks about the right to use and manage in the -- about four lines down in the English: "The right to use and ... manage, meaning that we are ... not interfering with the ownership. It would be regulated by a separate law ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the paragraph beginning: "Ergo ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Ergo, such a decree will allow anyone who returns to apply within 30 days, and in that case their property will not be the subject of sequester. If they fail to comply, then their property is sequestered. The problem of ownership shall be resolved in a separate law. This is another story." Now we have seen some debate, but in this session that you participated in, a wide variety of people weighed in on this debate. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think that the Chamber ultimately had the decree that was passed on 4 September 1995 which is P476, which allowed -- which mandates that 30 days be given for people to register and then the law itself, being D422, which was passed on 20 September 1995, again, that's D422, which moved that back up to 90 days. So, would it be accurate to say that we started early on in these debates with a lot of discussion as to what to do with that property and we move to a sequestration of 30, then 90 days, certainly by September of 1995, all within approximately a month period of time. Is that right? I mean, I don't want to put words in your mouth, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, isn't true that it I already put this to the witness, as what is known to the Chamber, I gave exactly the same dates. So therefore what is the use of asking the witness whether -- it is in evidence; we've seen it several times; and I told it to this witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it goes to the Chamber's comments, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you asked the witness whether it is right that this is what then followed. And I told the witness that that is in the knowledge of Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now when these discussions were taking place, was Ambassador Galbraith in these discussions, these private discussions, where how this law was going to be enacted was discussed among all these parties?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you as follows. We discussed this law widely. Many of us did not have any experience with the matter, but we did have our goal clearly in our minds, and this was to protect and preserve the property and to use it so that it wouldn't go to waste and also to protect private property. I don't remember that I personally met with Ambassador Galbraith at the time, but I certainly met with many representatives of the international community, and we tried to accord our proposals with them so that our proposals be internationally acceptable. I can remind you that on one occasion in a conversation that I had with Madam Albright when she told me that we had to prevent torching of the houses, I told her, of course, and we are do that, not because are you asking us to do that but because this is in line with our principles, and this is in line with our constitution. We have to prevent torching of the houses, looting. We have to protect private property. And we, at the same time, had to use that property to the best of our abilities during this very harsh times, when we had so many displaced in Croatia, from Croatia and from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and those that came from Bosnia-Herzegovina were both Croats and Bosniaks. So instead of them living in sport halls, under tents, in hotels, where we received them temporarily, the guiding idea was to protect the property, the main idea was if you have a family living in a house, that house will be protected, and we wanted to use them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radic, let me cut this short. The Chamber asked you a question concerning testimony given to the Court by Ambassador Galbraith, and that is at page 27159 to 27160 in various paragraphs, that this Law on the temporary taking over of Property was simply a pretext for permanently taking the property of the Serbs who left. What is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith is known to have been very superficial, and he did not have a sufficient insight into this problem. He may have said that this was a pretext for something else, but this is certainly not true. I personally coordinated this work, possibly he observed this from the side, but I can clearly confirm here what was the main idea and the main goal of this takeover of the property. The idea was to protect the property and not to destroy it, and it was certainly not a pretext to prevent anybody from returning. If that was our wish, then the simplest way would have been to torch down everything. But you could have seen here that I said directly to the President, We have to prevent torching. The President confirmed this. And I can also testify here that we had at least 50 such conversations in which we said, Let us protect all the property, let us prevent them from burning it down, because this is the property that is valuable for all the citizens of Croatia. So we would not have prevented the torching if our goal was to prevent people from coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I earlier asked you not to put questions such that you would elicit the same evidence from the witness already. Your last question, what your response is to the pretext, is aiming at an explanation on what was aimed at with this law. I think the witness has explained to this to us now three times, and we don't neat a fourth or a fifth time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that vein, I was going back to the question asked by the Chamber which, for a variety of reasons, wasn't answered squarely. I turn to that page, ask the Chamber to look at it, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the last document on this issue, P475. Now, this is the law on the change of the law of the temporary taking over and administration of specified property, and it notes in article 11 on the temporary take over and administration of specified property, paragraph 1 is changed and reads: "The issue of returning in possession and use of property which is under the ownership from Article 2 of this property must be regulated by the agreement of the normalisation of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And this is dated 17 January, 1996. So consistent with what we heard from minister Granic both the returns of people coming back, Serbs returning back, as well as ownership of property were not going to be dealt with until relations were being normalised. That was your understanding, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is what this law says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now briefly just going back to what we talked and you just touched upon, and we will abbreviate there discussion, which is the force 63, page 4 of 37, we don't need to read that again, where you're talking about the burning of property. I mean, you just addressed that with us, that you talked this about being the worse evil, and President Tudjman says, It should have been prevented from the beginning. I mean, this is a private conversation. Why were you saying that, sir? Give us the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two reasons. The first one is that I was president of the commission for return for the new creation of life in that area. This was a state commission appointed by the government at the time. So I spoke from that position. But also, in addition to that, I personally visited all these liberated areas, so I spoke about what I saw with my own eyes on the day of the assumption of the Virgin Mary, I saw that houses were burning in Cviljane, and I told President that this was no good. He asked me who were burning them. And I said, Well, these were different thieves, people who put on military uniforms, but they are not members of the army. And I told him if he go to the main square in the city of Zagreb you will see people walking around in uniforms who are not members of the army. So this was such a time, immediately after the war, when everybody could hide behind this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You condemned this in private, and you also made public statements condemning this as well, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I did it on many occasions, both directly, in my interviews for television during the sessions of the government and elsewhere. And I had full support for this from the President of the country, the prime minister, and the entire government. So this was my sincere personal belief, but this was not only my position, this was also the position of the President of the country and the entire leadership of the country. My task was reconstruction, and if we are talking about reconstructing houses, then it is better to preserve the houses than to have to reconstruct them entirely later on. This is why we wanted to protect all of the homes as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to one of your public statements on this score, 65 ter 1D3058. This is a newspaper article from the 23rd of August, 1995, one day after your discussion -- one day after your discussion that we just looked at in P463. I'm not certain that we have a B/C/S version of this so I will just read it to you in English, sir. And this is a document from Tanjug from the 23rd of August where it notes that you, "Croatian Deputy Prime Minister Jure Radic said Wednesday that Serb property in Krajina was being looted and destroyed." "Radic told the Croatian government session that he disassociated himself from these instances. Radic, on behalf of the government, proposed that the defence and the interior ministries be put in charge of preventing such conduct and punishing the perpetrators of these crimes. "Radic claimed that these crimes had not been committed by ... the army or the police but by those who followed military actions and plundered and destroyed the property." Mr. Radic, would this date and the substance of this message that in these newspaper articles comport with your memory about your public condemnation of this conduct?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates and the core message is as I recall it. Obviously, every journalist reports that in their own manner. But I spoke on several occasions in those days about the fact that we had to protect the property, and I sincerely wanted this message to be received by every single cross citizen who could contribute to the property being preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll to offer 65 ter 1D3058.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D02021.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2021 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, were you with President Tudjman in Karlovac when he gave a speech where he likewise publicly condemned the destruction of property in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring on the occasion when we travelled with train, the so-called train of liberty towards Split, yes, I was present. I was present on several occasions when President gave out this message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for reference without going into it, that's D1451, the 26th August video of President Tudjman condemning this destruction. Now, Mr. President, I will tell what you I intended to because it comports with some testimony that the witness had given before, and I will just lay it out. We have obviously seen a video from Mr. Liborius where he talks at some time about Kistanje being destroyed and construction commenced in 1996, he actually says that, and that, of course, comports with what Mr. Radic has said there here. That, of course, was what I was going lead into next which, of course, goes back to the transcript at page 5 where the witness says that this is preventing us from putting in houses -- by destroying this property, it's preventing us from putting displaced people in the houses. I raise this to the Chamber because, of course, I want to be guided by what the Chamber is looking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few questions in which you're focussing on what was said in the transcripts, and if even if the Chamber has not specifically dealt with looting and burning, is -- you have an opportunity to do that. But let's clearly [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's clearly understand then, an important matter in this case, apparently is what was said, when, where, what was done, what followed, what was known to happen on the ground. And that is a rather complex matter. The Chamber focussed very much on hearing the evidence of a witness who had attended some of the meetings which were not public and which had been on our table many, many times. And, therefore, the Chamber, as was clearly said, I think in our guidance, is that -- that we did not intend to seek any further evidence on the legislative activities. For example, we knew what the follow-up steps were in legislation. We have seen it; we have heard about it, planning, developing, implementing programmes. The focus primarily was to see whether the knowledge of this witness on what happened during these meetings could make us better understand what was said during these meetings. I'm fully aware that we could question this witness for weeks on all the other matters he may have knowledge of. That was not primarily the reason the Chamber called this witness. And, apparently, the parties have refrained from calling him for that purpose. That, more or less, sets the context and the boundaries for the examination. I think I already told you that -- if you -- of course, we have -- most of the evidence is clearly on our minds. I can't say that every detail of it is always without having to verify that. But if there's anything said about looting and burning, where we heard already very, very often, let's -- let there be no question about that, that the last thing that would be in the interest of Croatia was that houses would be burned and looted. Because whatever your approach would have been to who would live in there, et cetera, I leave that now entirely -- and from a neutral point of view, if you want people to live there, you better have houses that are not destroyed and which are not looted. That's -- we have heard that many, many times, and from the whole -- I think this witness told us this already in between one of the previous answers. I think three or four answers from now, he already referred to that, so that is not new for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I, of course, am talking about Kistanje because the Chamber yesterday mourning did in fact discuss Kistanje, the destruction of Kistanje, and the reconstruction efforts so that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most important was that the Chamber, although it had seen the statement of the witness, that if you say there was a reconstruction programme where houses were built, if you don't know when it happened, what form it took, that the information in that statement would be entirely without meaning for us whether that was in 2002, whether it was in 1997, 1996, 1999, so, therefore, you may also have noted that the Chamber sought specific, very factual information and then did not follow up that much, just what are we talking about, and that was it. And didn't go much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My comment to that is this, Mr. President. My understanding in your questioning was going an intent element.
