And, of course, the intent element in this case is multi-faceted and in various different areas. So it was exactly to that degree that we were trying to get a named member of the JCE to give the Chamber additional information not only the intent element that the Chamber raised but other aspects of it but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if would you have liked to do that, you should have called the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the Chamber called the witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and he was here with limited purposes and gave guidance to the parties, as it did not intend to go through all of the evidence. As I said before, we could hear evidence of this witness for weeks and weeks. You decided not to call him. The Chamber decided to limit the scope of his examination, fully aware that there would have been larger areas, and that's where we are, and that's what we expect the parties to join in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I understand that, Mr. President, and certainly I agree with you, Mr. President, that we could be here for weeks going through a cross-examination. And I do believe given the fact that my cross-examination is almost complete that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I allowed you to put a few questions on a certain matter, rather than to enter into a debate which takes more time than just asking the witness those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's why I raised issuing concerning Kistanje. I'm just trying to get into the issue of there was a reconstruction, there's a video that show it is very briefly, he went back there and started constructing them in 1996. You know, when did you start constructing, and whose houses were you reconstructing, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if we would look at the reconstruction, again the Chamber already said that they were not that much interested in the programmes that then followed. That was not -- we specifically and negatively said, This is not what we are seeking. I read to you. We said: "The Chamber is not intending to seek any further evidence on legislative activities or on planning, developing, or implementing programmes," and then we added on which the Chamber has already received extensive evidence, and then we name persons. Now this apparently is an element which is a new little programme that -- or a big programme which we had not heard about yet. We saw a reference to that in the statement of the witness, and we asked ourselves, Is this something entirely new? What is it? And then we got the time-frame. We got more or less the context of what it was, and we had no further questions on it. Now, Ms. Gustafson, if -- if we would see some construction workers building, I think, there were 150 or 250 houses, would that cause you a lot of preparation for further examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I doubt I would be interested in following up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed. But I would rather keep you to your time-limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned to us yesterday, Mr. Radic, that there was a reconstruction that commenced in Kistanje in 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said as I recall it was in 1996, but we started a reconstruction in various areas at various times. But as far as I recall, it was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the question. Answer that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a very brief video from a former ECMM monitor, P842, and this is just an excerpt from this. And this is Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "My name is Soren Liborius. I worked with ECMM during and after Operation Storm in August 1995. We are now approaching the town of Kistanje in former Sector South from the road from Knin. Kistanje used to be a Serb strong hold where the majority by far being Serbs. Kistanje was burned immediately after Operation Storm, in fact the burning began during the first day of the 5th of August. "When the first international organisations personnel drove through Kistanje it was many houses on flames, and the burning of houses and facilities in Kistanje continued throughout the month of August. The intensity in the burning was clearly in the first week after the 4th, 5th of August. "What we see now is a lot of reconstruction efforts going on, and we will see many houses with new roofs, new windows, new doors. The majority of the population is now ethnic Croats, either from the region of Kosovo in Yugoslavia, or Croat DPs returning, or Bosnian Croats being allowed temporarily use of accommodation here. "We will see the new terra cotta tiles on the roofs. These are reconstructed in the autumn of 1996 and the spring of 1997, and the appearance of the Kistanje town is very different now to what it was in the summer of 1995 and also in August 1996."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, as part of your programme that you noted in the video note began in 1996, whose houses were you rebuilding?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's quite a serious misunderstanding if Their Honours will allow me to explain. I said that in 1996 we started the construction of new buildings in Kistanje to which we moved the people who were put up temporarily. And in 1995, as can be seen in this video, the reconstruction started of partly damaged or destroyed houses. And it is not correct what was said here that the majority of houses were destroyed. A smaller number were destroyed and they were repaired, and for most of them they required a little reconstruction for temporary inhabitants to be put up there. So there were two projects for Kistanje. One was the reconstruction, so we call them Serb houses that were less damaged, and the construction of a new part of the settlement to which we moved people. The reconstruction started immediately in 19995. You see here the that was canal was dug for electricity, water, and everything else. And then in 1996, we started with the construction of the new 150 houses, so that Kistanje today is twice the size what it was. There are twice as many houses now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kay -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions from the Cermak Defence. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will only have a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, Mr. Mikulicic will now cross-examine you. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will put to you only a couple of questions, so please answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Radic, we see from the statement that you gave to the counsel for General Gotovina that, from about 1992 until 2003, you were engaged in politics in various capacities. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have also seen that you performed some important political and party duties in the Republic of Croatia, so my question is: Whether, in that capacity, you met with the highest level officials in politics and party life of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. It was part of my life for 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would that include the President of the republic, the president of the parliament, the prime minister, the ministers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I was head of the office of the president of the republic for two and a half years, and daily we would spend hours an hours together. I would often travel with him when we toured various areas and, of course, I would meet with all the other colleagues of mine in the state authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, The indictment against the accused, Gotovina, Cermak, and Markac, in this Tribunal, says that they, together with other persons, and those are the persons that we have just mentioned, and that you met on a daily basis, that they were all involved in a joint criminal enterprise, the aim of which to permanently remove the Serb population from the region Krajina by force, by threat, through intimidation, persecution, forced resettlement and deportation, destruction of property, and in other ways. My question: Did you ever, Mr. Radic, in performing your official duties in the political life of the Republic of Croatia as a minister in the government, as the vice premier, as the head of the president's office, as a leader in the HDZ, as a parliamentary deputy, did you ever participant in such a plan as described by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and never. I repeat that three times because it is incompatible with my outlook on the world, and I never heard anything like that within the circle that we have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, putting the Prosecution's case in the broadest of possible terms and asking the witness to confirm or deny that is far beyond the limited topics of examination that the Chamber set out in its e-mail to the parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just citing the Article 12 from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what Ms. Gustafson is telling you -- is telling me, that you shouldn't do that. You could also ask the witness whether the accused are guilty or not, and then read the whole of the indictment. That's -- of course, I'm not exaggerating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm exaggerating; I'm saying that. But this apparently is not within the boundaries of what the Chamber expected the parties to remain in. Apart from that, composite questions not having two, three, or four elements, but likely 20 factual elements and 10 legal elements in it, and then to ask the witness yes or no is really not assisting the Chamber in reaching the determinations it will have to make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, were you aware of any such criminal plan?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the first part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. Ms. Gustafson, I take it will have a similar objection to your question. The Chamber called the witness to ask clarification of certain matters -- not to ask whether you could ask every witness, Are you aware of any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... Your Honour, the witness is part of the -- central government and central political bodies in Croatia at that time, so he is not everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, and, therefore, you could have called him. You didn't. And apart from that, the answer -- I mean, where there is a possibility, are you aware of any criminal plans in which apparently then, first of all, I think we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There is the court of the indictment, and the procedure we are sitting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we are seeking as a matter of fact facts. Now can you ask the witness, did you attend a meeting in which Mr. A or B said this? But just so say -- you could ask him was there a joint criminal enterprise, more or less. That's -- again, I'm exaggerating, but let's focus on facts, and let's also focus on the subject matter for which the Chamber called the witness. Apart from that, Ms. Gustafson, there's no need. Mr. Mikulicic said that he would have ten minutes of questioning for the witness. If the questions are of this kind, then rather than objecting, you also could say, Well, we'll hear the answers which, I would say, follow. And I mean, if Mr. Radic was of the opinion that there were criminal [indiscernible] at that time, I think he would not -- if he would ever express that, or if he -- all his answers go in a different direction. He explained the -- how reasonable certain plans were. And then to say, Was there a criminal plan? No, he has explained to us how reasonable it all was. So, therefore, it's a superfluous question. It doesn't assist us. It is beyond the boundaries of what the witness said. At the same time, Ms. Gustafson, I encourage you in view of my -- and let me check ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I checked with my colleagues, to object to questions, questions I just said would not in any way assist the Chamber in reaching its determinations may be a waste of time, but then objecting to it may be a waste of time as well. Mr. Mikulicic has asked for ten minutes, and he may continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have only one last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, you told us that you were not aware of such a project. Would have you been aware of it in view of the positions that you held and the contacts you had with the highest officials of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about it. I certainly would have known, because, for a while, I was number 2 and number 3 in the Croatian state. I also head of the office and secretary of the party, so in view of my positions in the very top echelons of government, I wouldn't have necessarily known if any such project had existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Mr. Radic. Questioned by the Court: The first one is about what you were asked about, the conversation about Plaski and Saborski. You remember Ms. Gustafson asked was Plaski a Serb village? Was Saborski a Croatian village? There had been some discussion as to having to move twice, first to Plaski and then back to Saborski. Then the discussion went on in which it was said there was strong opposition against moving twice, suggesting that there could be reasons for those who had moved in to Plaski to stay there. And then you drew our attention to the fact that in Plaski there may well have been apartments so that not moving out of Plaski could well be explained by apartments being there which were state owned. And then you said it's very easy to establish that. Now, just for a transparency of the parties, I now and then look at Google Earth. I will usually tell you when I do that. Now looking at the village of Plaski very much gives an impression of being a mainly rural area, and as far as can you see from above, there seemed to be not much of -- of apartment blocks. Nevertheless, you used that as a possible explanation, why people would stay in Plaski. You also told us that it would be easy to verify. How would you verify that? About the presence of state-owned apartments in this village.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you that it is easy to verify. I think I went to Plaski two or three times in my life, and I remember in the centre of Plaski there are several housing buildings, apartment buildings. Maybe there were about ten or so apartments. Plaski, like Saborski is an area mainly inhabited by forestry workers. It is an area where forest are exploited and some of the apartments were owned by the Croatian forests company, and also teachers had state-owned apartments, and so on. But the main idea behind your question obviously was, Let us bring people from Saborski close to their own village so that they could assist in the reconstruction. The most successful achievements were those in which the participants took part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to tell me what the main idea behind my questions. What my ideas behind my questions is, either I share them with the parties, but it is not for you to speculate on that. But I'm quite willing to tell you, you gave a certain explanation as to why not moving out could be -- would not in any way affect rights of individual owners of houses, because it could well be that people who didn't then want to move out again could stay in state-owned apartments. Now, I was just trying to verify the factual basis for that explanation, which is how many state-owned apartments are there in Plaski and how to verify that. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Along those lines, Mr. President, I think there may be an interpretation with the last sentence of the first full paragraph of the witness's last answer, which on my LiveNote is page 58, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll verify that because my recollection is that I heard something different. You told us that you had seen in the centre of Plaski apartments. Could you tell us a bit more in detail, were these apartment blocks, were there -- how many were there?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid my memory is not so precise, because in those days, I toured all the Croatian villages, but I certainly remember that in the centre of Plaski there were some houses that were apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes and could you --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But their number, I'm afraid I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I know of apartment buildings, and we have seen many of them, Bosansko Grahovo, Knin, et cetera, we have seen a lot of pictures of apartment buildings. Could you tell us approximately how many apartments in each building, as far as your recollection serves you?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking about Plaski?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much fewer in relation to the towns that you have just mentioned. Much fewer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but are we talking about buildings with four apartments, or 12, or 30, or ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression from this time distance, and this was happening some 15 years ago, there may have been buildings with about ten apartments, not more than that. Several buildings of that size, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say ten apartments, how many of these apartment buildings or blocks would have been there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several. Several. I can't remember with precision. But this can easily be verified and checked. This was certainly not a large number. There may have been 20 to 30 apartments that were state owned. Maybe that would be my approximation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get a picture for myself as to -- to what extent your explanation of people staying in the state-owned apartments would be. Now, if there would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I don't know if we are talking about two different pieces of Google Earth, but we have pulled up the map of Google Earth in Plaski who has a multitude of item there, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... on the same page, is that the one with the paper factory in there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is one factory, at least there seems to be one industrial complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't have it in front of me as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Over to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way of showing this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Via Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Via Sanction. Then we could ask the witness do point to -- yes, this seems to be -- this is -- could we perhaps zoom out a bit. I said "a bit." Yes, Witness, could you tell us, you see here an aerial view of the village of Plaski where these apartment blocks were located approximately? If your recollection serves you.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is that place. At the time I was in the centre of that settlement. Now, where that is I absolutely cannot remember. It has faded in my memory. But I can confirm that at least 30 families could be accommodated in these state-owned apartments or state institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I did understand that it was a village of some -- also looking at you, Ms. Gustafson, 2.000 inhabitants, I think it was said. Thirty families would amount to anything between 100 and 150 persons. Is that -- I'm trying to get a picture of -- to what extent this explanation, what it exactly would mean. I now understand then that that would be approximately 7 to 8 per cent, rough estimate, of the accommodations which, as being state-owned apartments, could explain why people would -- could stay there without occupying any private property. Is that -- are we on the same line on that?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we are talking about the inhabitants of Saborski that needed to be put up in Plaski. Inhabitants of Saborski in Plaski and from the standpoint of reconstruction if certain families or some 50 men who can take part in the work, that is a considerable achievement. For us every single family was very important for us. The people from Saborski, at about 200 metres altitude higher than Plaski, many of them were working across the hill in another place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you're focussing on matters which are different from my issue. The discussion was about Saborski being destroyed. Temporarily moving Saborski which was a mainly Croat village to Plaski which was not destroyed, in a similar way, and that there was at least -- there were objections against then having to move again out of Plaski to Saborski, and then it was suggested to you in the questioning by Ms. Gustafson that, if people didn't want to move out from Plaski, that they would then, for a longer period of time, occupy Serb accommodations. And then you said, But don't forget that there were state-owned apartments in there, and I was just trying to figure out the quantitative aspect of your answer. I have no further questions for you. Unless you would like to add something, but where people were working was not of direct relevance for what I sought to establish for myself.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to add. I think I answered all your questions. And I leave here with the impression that have I tried to demonstrate the main idea behind reconstruction and return, which was open, and designed for all Croatian citizens, and from today's perspective --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not there yet. I asked you whether there was anything to as to my last question. Ms. Gustafson, is there any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few questions, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Ms. Gustafson:

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P463, please; and page 4 in the English, and page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radic, again we're going back to the 22nd of August, 1995 conversation you had with President Tudjman. And I'd like to move down to -- towards the bottom of the page where you begin: "However one thing I have to tell you ..." And this is where you inform President Tudjman that you visited the area by car and by helicopter, and you say: "Our men torched a lot ..." and that conversation continues.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now when you said: "However, one thing I have to tell you," it appears that you are, at this point, notifying President Tudjman of what had seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, without doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you had -- you were explaining to him what you had seen. And if we move to the next page in the English, you talk about Kijevo and Civljane. And you said: "I got there on the day of Assumption of the Virgin Mary to find everything has been burned down. And I assume you're talking about Civljane there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the Day of Assumption, is that the 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "It's not the army, it's that fifth echelon, which is under, I don't know whose, what kind of banner. Put on a uniform, wander around." And at the end of that paragraph you say: "I am not telling hearsay, but the things I have experienced myself and seen with my own eyes, torching and looting." Did you see people in uniform torching and looting when you visited the area?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I went by road from Sinj to Knin. And the village of Kijevo and Civljane are by the road but a couple of hundred metres away from the road. And I saw the smoke rising from the houses, and this is what I told the President about. I did not see the person burning down. This was done probably during the night. But I saw the houses burning, and this is what I informed the President about. And I said this was no good, and he agreed with me. I also told him that I visit the some small town, Drnis, Benkovac, and so forth, and that there this was not happening; but in the villages I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you say you just saw smoke. So why did you refer to people putting on a uniform, wandering about, the worst tramps, torching and looting. Why mention people in uniform if, as you say, you didn't see any people at all conducting this activity?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my conclusion because I knew that both the army and the civilian police would have prevented civilians from entering this area. But if somebody came there at this time in a military uniform, and I -- as I told the President at that time, even at the main square of the city of Zagreb, square of Ban Jelacic, you could see people wearing uniforms, but these were not members of the army; these were people who were hiding behind these uniforms in order to be able to loot and then burn. This is what was happening in some of the villages, and my position was that we had to prevent this. But to answer your question, I did not see people physically burning. This was my conclusion, which I then conveyed to the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if it is your conclusion, because you knew that the army and the police would have prevented civilians from entering the area, but you also knew that it was -- or concluded that it was not members of the army looting and burning, how is that possible? If there is no civilians in the area, how is it possible that it's not the army looting and burning?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said that were my impressions and my conclusions. I knew how our army was organised. I knew how disciplined it was, and I was convinced that it was impossible, apart from maybe some exceptional cases, but I thought it was impossible for this to happen in any organised manner. This was, as far as my knowledge went, and I believe the President shared this view, because such a person would have been immediately punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So your conclusion that it wasn't the real army conducting this activity is based on your view that the HV was disciplined and organised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the information that I had from many of my colleagues and friends who were commanders in the army, and it was also based on my discussions with them. For example, my deputy from my ministry went to the army. He put on the uniform and went to defend Croatia, and I knew that anybody who was led by such a person could not have done things of the kind, and I spoke to him during those days as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And which particular colleagues and friends who were commanders in the army told you that it wasn't the army looting and burning? And when exactly did they tell you that? Names and dates.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the secretary in my minister, Marijan Perkovic, who later became brigadier of the Croatian Army and now is he back at the ministry, he is one that told me such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was his position at the time after Operation Storm or at the of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Operation Storm, he came back to be secretary of the ministry of reconstruction and development, and he is the one who physically drafted the laws on return and similar laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was his position in the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. He may have led a battalion, or a unit of that kind. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber considers that it is not further assisted by exploring specifically these sources, and thinks that the point you apparently would like to make is sufficiently made by the -- by pointing at conclusions and sources for those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And it appears from the transcript of this conversation that President Tudjman was not particularly surprised by the information you were providing him. And I'd like to ask you, as far as -- as far as you are aware, did President Tudjman already know about looting and burning in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the first thing you put to the witness that from the transcript that it appears that he was not surprised. Now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you please take out that portion of the question and, of course, the second portion of the question is you're asking about facts. But the first one is, to say the least, has a bit of an unstable basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now my question, Mr. Radic, was it your impression at the time that President Tudjman already knew about the looting and burning; or when you told him about this, did you think that he was hearing this for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From his very answer when he said, I keep saying that this should be prevented, it follows that somebody else told him the same thing, and he probably answered in the same manner in which he answered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about public statements you made, condemning the destruction, and one in particular or a report of one was shown to you. And it seems from your -- the statement you gave to the Gotovina Defence that you attended a meeting on the 12th of August in Drnis and that by the 12th of August -- or on the 12th of August, you visited the -- the area liberated by Operation Storm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that I was there, but I actually chaired that meeting in Drnis. This was the second meeting of the state staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not so interested in the contents of the meeting. I'm more interested in where you were on the 12th of August. And it's clear you were in Drnis --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where did you come from to get to Drnis, and how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I can't remember how I came, where from. Too much time has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would it have been by road?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so. I'm just trying to remember whether I came from Zagreb or whether I was in Split at the time and came there from Split. I can't recall that. At that time, I visited the field on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you have travelled along the route between Knin and Drnis on that day?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether I passed from Knin to Drnis. I think so, but I can't say that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And on the 12th of August, when you were travelling through the area, did you see any signs of ongoing or recent destruction of property, such as houses burning, columns of smoke, looting? Any signs that there might have been recent destruction of property, on the 12th of August, when you were -- went to Drnis?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I seen that, probably I would have informed the President about this couple of days later. But I took out the example of what I saw on the 15, and I remember that I described to him the situation, that I saw in Drnis where we, indeed, found many destroyed houses particularly in the villages surrounding Drnis. Had I seen any torching along my way to Drnis, I probably would have informed the President about this, as I did inform him about what I saw on the 15th. So from this I can only draw the conclusion that I came by road from Split to Drnis which passes through Cavoglave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, we're also now slowly moving a bit away from the meetings and getting into personal observation. Now, to some extent, the example given on the 15th is clear. That's part of the minutes. I would like to avoid that you further enter into the area of personal observation during these days or several areas because that is not exactly within the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it arose out of the cross-examination that was permitted by the Bench, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, just one other brief topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In cross-examination, you were shown a clip of Minister Granic speaking, and the proposition was put to you that the return of Serbs would depend -- or that the -- that the position of the Croatian authorities was that the return of Serbs would depend on the normalisation of relations with the FRY except for individual humanitarian cases. And yesterday I -- you -- we looked at the 1996 Law on Areas of Special State Concern, and you asserted that the goal of this law was not limited to bringing Croats into the area and that it included within its scope the Serbs who had left the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just perhaps before -- I know that you are on your feet. Perhaps you wait first until Ms. Gustafson has phrased her question, but I already ask the witness not to answer the question until we have heard Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And according to your testimony today, and -- and just preliminarily when this Law on Areas of Special State Concern was enacted, there was no agreement on normalisation of relations. And according to your testimony today, the position of the Croatian authorities at the time this law was passed was that the Croatian Serbs outside Croatia could not return except for individual humanitarian cases. So this law when it was passed could not have been aimed at encouraging Croatian Serbs to return because their return was not permitted at that time. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection to this, Mr. President, is that we never asked the question about the Law on Areas of Special State Concern. So in the spirit of the objections that have been levied on my cross-examination, it's similar to this. We never went into this area at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It wasn't -- I was trying to contrast what the witness said today in response to a question from the cross-examination with what he said yesterday. I think it's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer your question now? So, once again, we are talking about two levels or two different things. One of them is the agreement on normalisation which would talk about mass return. And a second issue is daily processing of applications by Serbs who, in the meantime, accepted Croatian citizenship, and they were coming back to Croatia. In Vukovar, President Tudjman said that there were 14.500 such cases. So when we are talking about individual cases, this turned into a rather large number. So we were talking about thousands of people who came back. So this doesn't collide with this other issue. The law allowed it for everybody to return, but in practice, obviously, we had to resolve individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, President Tudjman was talking about -- in Vukovar was talking about people who were returning from even Slavonia, not people who were returning from outside Croatia. But here you're saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, is that a question or a speech? I object. That -- that is -- if is question --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's foundation to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, is it -- do you contest that President Tudjman was talking about 14.500?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Gustafson understands -- excuse me, Mr. President -- the premise of what he was saying, that thousands of people came in for humanitarian reasons, thousands of people, we're not talking about a handful. With that core concept of his answer, I think a question can come from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, perhaps not the most expeditious way, but -- would have been to take the witness back to that specific portion and read it and then establish what President Tudjman was talking about and then to phrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That would be P2536. At page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the first full paragraph in Croatian, and it's the paragraph that begins: "Ladies and gentlemen ..." And President Tudjman, as you see says: "All those Serbs who are citizens of Croatia, who have taken Croatian citizenship and who are living in this county and the neighbouring Osijek-Baranja county and the entire Danubian area, if they want to return to their homes in the western parts of Croatia, from Pakrac to Knin, they will be allowed to return. About 14.500 have already returned. If they do not wish [sic] to return, we shall give them compensation so that they can go wherever they wish." He is talking about Serbs from Eastern Slavonia returning to western parts of Croatia; right? Not Serbs outside Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is talking about a total number of people who will come back to the area between Knin, Pakrac, and other areas, and who are now somewhere else. We need to agree on the fact that when people left after the Storm, some of them moved to Serbia and some of them moved to the Danube region. The border between Croatia and Yugoslavia at that time was open. They behaved as if it was one and the same state. So we did not know where Croats -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Where Serbs from Knin went.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... whether they went to Danube region or to Serbia, because the border between the Danube region and Serbia were under their control, not under ours. And only after the reintegration of the Danube region could we control that border. So the data that we did have was that 14.500 Serbs came back to the liberated area, and at that time they all enjoyed all the privileges granted to them by the Law on Areas of Special State Concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a rule under Italian law of criminal procedure which allows the Defence always to put the last question to the witness. Now that rule doesn't apply, because what Judges usually do under those circumstances is to put another question to the witness and then the Defence will. Now that is not what we are aiming at at this moment but, Judge Kinis has another question for the witness and I may have one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I have quite short question to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You mention that you travelled around area on 15th of August, and recognised many atrocities on the ground. You also mentioned that one of concerns for returning people in mass way was security issues, including mines on the ground, and booby-traps maybe in buildings, and so on and so forth. How could you explain that after on 15th August that full freedom of movement were allowed for this area for Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I didn't catch this question that it was allowed or that it wasn't allowed? Could you just clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: On 15th of August, Chamber receives all the evidence on this respect, that all -- full freedom of movement were allowed for Croatian citizens to go in this liberated area and to move and go out and in and so. And why under this situation you didn't -- state leadership didn't care about security of those people?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full freedom of movement was certainly not granted. I was deputy prime minister of the Croatian government, and I was stopped at a check-point and controlled. So, obviously, there were certain controlled check-points or parameters, but if some people passed over some hills to come there, this is what I based my conclusion on, that these were some criminals that engaged in looting and not regular citizens. So there were main check-points, control points, but this is such a large area that our police force simply could not have it all under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I think that you are not correct, because Chamber already receives evidence and including this order which allow full freedom of movement for citizens after 15th of August, and first train was organised from Split to Knin directly on this date. That's why I'm thinking that your answer is not correct on this -- on this respect.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it well, that I was stopped myself near the village of Hrvatse [phoen] and that they asked me where I was going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if -- if I have a feeling that there may be some mal-communication. What Judge Kinis is talking about is that Croats could move into the area again. That at least how I understood his question. Train, people arriving, no prohibition to travel around. Not to say that there were not, at times, and at occasions, check-points, areas which may have been closed for certain kind of operations. But the question of Judge Kinis apparently says: Why could the Croats return, even if they would be stopped at check-points; and why was de-mining, et cetera, not a safety concern which resulted in saying, Stay out, we're not ready yet; whereas for Serbs, apparently the security concerns contributed considerably to the policy that they could not return freely as they wished.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. There was some noise in the headphones, I didn't fully understand the question. Through the media, we kept warning people that it was still not time for the return. The return has to be organised. But, of course, as soon as it was possible to open the road from Zagreb to Split, not for Croats but for all Croatian citizens, you had to show your ID. The ID doesn't say whether I am a Serb or a Croat, but whether I'm a Croatian citizen. Instead of travelling some 500 or 600 kilometres from Split to Zagreb, you could do it in 400 kilometres. So we -- the first chance we had, we opened the road and the railway for travel. But we warned people that you still cannot go back to your homes, but I gave you the example today that a man got killed because he went there and tried to do some cleaning, and he was killed. So we kept warning the people that the return would be an organised process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any document or any minutes of meetings in which it is stated, or is there any other clear evidence in which it is stated, although there's no question about your Croatian citizenship, don't come back to your village because it is not safe. Could you give us examples of where you said you warned the population? It may well be that it is even somewhere in the evidence. I'm not quite certain about it. But I'm asking you, since you referred to such warnings.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We quoted this today, I think, that the Defence showed such a document in which I say in public at an open session of the government about this. I think it was on the screen today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was the meeting that I referred to. I believe it is 1813 on the 7th of -- if can I just get one second, I can give you the exact page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is -- it's a discussion that takes place at various times in D813, I didn't go through all of the items, but Minister Radic, this is 28 in the English. Excuse me, it is not 28 in the English. It starts page 11, so that would be 17 in the English, and -- 18 in the English, and that's where he talks about, People can't come back -- you know, spontaneous returnees can't rush back, we have t o organise things. That's just one that I think that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I'm primarily looking at the warnings being given in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was a public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that is different from addressing the public. That's -- But Mr. Kehoe has drawn our attention to a place where this was discussed. Could you add any other document or evidence or, was it said on television or ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I don't have those documents, but I remember well that I visited the refugees from those settlements and told them in person that they should wait, that we need to have an organised return, on several occasions and in several places, and it is impossible that there are no media reports about this, but I personally don't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you. If the further questions have not triggered any need, then, yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One issue on that. Further cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, after Operation Storm, why didn't the Republic of Croatia just completely seal off the liberated area? Why didn't they do that?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aim was life. For five years, people lived as refugees and they couldn't wait to return to their homes. So we must bear in mind that several hundreds of thousands of Croats had spent five years as refugees, and when the Storm came, for them, it was like a second birthday, and they couldn't wait to see whether their house was intact, whether they could return. And what kind of a government would we be if we were to seal it off now that have you lived to see liberation, we want to let you go home but, on the other hand, we also had to take into account serious security concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: According to Italian criminal procedure, last question was put by you. Mr. Radic. Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to inform the Chamber, it is exactly the same position in the Croatian criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I still have to learn a lot, as you see. But this was adopted later than 1991, when the Italian new code of criminal procedure was adopted. Mr. Radic, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the Bench and that were put to you by the parties, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am very happy if I have made even a small contribution to clear up understanding of the just struggle in the homeland war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Radic out of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that the folder is still there or -- one second. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had on my agenda, but I left them until after the testimony of this witness, a few procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I address a couple of issues related to this witness before Your Honours shifts gears, very briefly. I mean, I just want to advise the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have to come back after a break anyhow, then we could do it after a break as well, because we are at a point where --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we would have taken a break already a while ago. So, therefore, let me just. Yes, I have a few procedural questions which will not take a lot of time. Most likely some 15 to 20 minutes. How much time would you need, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just 30 seconds, Mr. President, just two issues briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is really 30 seconds, then I would invite to you do it now, so that we can then after the break deal with procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, Mr. President, I'll start. First, in Plaski there are 187 state-owned apartments, 90 per cent of them owned by the factory. We can make a bar table submission on that. Second, I have been advised by one of my colleagues that there is a transcript 65 ter 939 from December 1995 where General Cervenko notes that 400 returnees have been killed by mines, and we will provide that to the Chamber as well. I think I'm within the 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are. I'm afraid that interpreters and transcribers have paid the price for that. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to start this -- well, it's not a real housekeeping session, but at least we're dealing with mainly administrative matters with P2712. Mr. Kehoe, you objected against admission due to disclosure. It has been MFI'd. It was during the examination of Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I haven't taken a look at it since that time, I still reserve my objection, but I will get back to the Chamber in short order by e-mail and with counsel as to our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait for further messages from you. Then we briefly looked at Google Maps. Now the witness couldn't identify where he had seen these apartment blocks. Unless there's any objection, the Chamber considers there's no need to have this into evidence. I hear of no objections. Mr. Kehoe, you came with two numbers, I think 187 and 400 after the break. Well, the 400 is I think the same as what we saw already in the transcript, to that extent it corroborates or confirms. But I do not know whether there was any reason -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It was a transcript for December of 1995. I don't think has been admitted. But I do believe -- I'm corrected that you have seen it. That is, the transcript you have seen from December of 1995. That has the 400 people -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I read that portion from the transcript. I think 400, and we briefly discussed with the witness whether there were injured people or killed people. And it seems not to be something which is in dispute that 400 people may have been killed due to accidents with mines. Ms. Gustafson, seems not to be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly not that mines were an issue. I mean, I would have to look exactly at the transcript. We don't know what area we are talking about. But, no, as a general matter, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that de-mining after this war period was a serious problem that -- well, hardly is fit for dispute. Apart from all the details and it what caused and what it did not cause, et cetera, but I would say this comes close to common sense. The 187, Mr. Kehoe, the questioning was aiming at the situation in 1995. Is this information -- I don't know where it comes from. Is it related to the situation in 1995? I see Mr. Misetic is nodding yes. What's the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm advised that we are getting this from the Croatian ministry, from Mr. Radic's ministry on the number of apartments at that time. Certainly we will get those documents and give them to counsel to review before we attempt to bar table anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps look at it as a whole, because the testimony of the witness, we came to an assessment, a rough assessment which was, well, at least considerably lower because I multiplied the number of apartments, I think we're talking about, overall, 30 apartments, I think I counted 4 in a family. So we were talking, on the basis of the testimony of the witness, we were talking about seven or eight, approximately, per cent of the population in -- housed in apartments, whereas, of course, the number 187 is quite different, because if I multiply that by four, let's say, for an average family, then that would come to 550, approximately, which comes close to 25 per cent of the population, which would -- which would solidify the explanation given by the witness. So, therefore, since there is quite a gap between the two, the number are you giving comes down to almost -- approximately three and a half times more than what the witness -- his recollection was. Therefore, if we use this number and also having looked at the map where I would be -- well, where I was -- I was able to identify certain industrial facilities, and I could imagine of some of the features being what I know to be the normal feature of an apartment block, but 25 per cent is, of course, for the population is -- is quite a bit. So, therefore, if -- if would you rely on that, I would invite you to seek verification of this information and perhaps discuss it with the Prosecution before we finally move from what the witness told us to what you consider to be the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I move on matters unrelated to Witness Radic. The Gotovina Defence has e-mailed a precedent from a 2004 partial award of the Eritrea Ethiopia Claims Commission, which, as was said, it might use during the Radic cross-examination. The issue was whether or not we would then need that in evidence. Now, first, it was not used. But usually case law is -- if it's easily accessible through public sources needs not to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree. I was simply sending that -- or we were simply sending that on the idea that -- to give the Chamber and the parties some notification of our areas of cross-examination. So there would be some basis and certainly the Chamber wouldn't be surprised. We're not asking that the award be put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next, I would like to announce to the parties that in the week of the 5th to the 9th of April of this year, that there will be no sitting in the Gotovina case. That is, whatever other scheduling things may come up, that is the week, I would say, the spring week of not sitting, just for the parties to know already. I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. D215 is the transcript of the 277th Closed Session of the Government of the Republic of Croatia, which was held on the 5th of October, 1995. It was tendered through Witness Gojanovic on the 19th of May, 2008. At the housekeeping session at the 27th of January, the OTP stated that it would provide a full translation. I'm addressing the OTP. Is the full translation, meanwhile, available and has is been uploaded? Mr. Waespi or Ms. Gustafson, whoever is hiding behind the pillar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure, Your Honour. There is at least three different exhibit numbers that contain portions of this, and I think between all three of them there might be a complete translation. But I would have to verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say make it a jigsaw puzzle, we have three pieces, and put the picture together. I would rather stick to what was said by the OTP on 27th of January, and we'd like to hear from you once it has been uploaded, so that then the Registrar can be instructed to attach the full translation to D215. I move on to the -- to P2530. There was a B/C/S version missing. I do understand that the B/C/S version is uploaded. And, Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to attach the missing B/C/S version to the -- to Exhibit P2530. Then you're also instructed to replace the English version of this same exhibit, P2530, with the new English version with handwritten inserts. And, finally, you are instructed to attach the Prosecution's discrepancy report, in relation to P2530 to P2708 and, unless there are any objections, I will decide that P2708 is admitted into evidence. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, just consulting with Mr. Misetic, I'm not certain -- I'm not sure exactly what these are, candidly. Maybe I can get some help from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm informed that it is the annotated version of the Markac suspect interview transcripts, with the discrepancy reports. But I'm afraid I can't offer anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the advantage of the e-court system. If I give the numbers, you can just get them on your screen so that we know what we are talking about. It is, indeed -- it is the video and the transcript of the suspect interview with Mladen Markac, 3rd and 4th of March, 2003, partial. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe I exchanged an e-mail with the OTP office saying that have I nothing against introduction of this, translation of the written remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under those circumstances, the third part of my instructions, that is, to attach the Prosecution's discrepancy report in relation to P2530 to P2708, and that P2708 is admitted into evidence. Would you still like to look at P2708, Mr. Mikulicic, or is it clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is clear to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then just for ... yes. Then I would like to move on to a document -- well, it's not a document; it's an audio clip. The Galbraith audio clip, 1D33-074, was used by the Gotovina Defence with Witness Galbraith, and it is about a 19th of October, 1995, meeting attended by President Tudjman, Ambassador Galbraith, and Ambassador Holbrooke. First of all, let me verify, I have on my list here, 1D33-074, but a little bit later it states 0474.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the latter, Mr. President. It's the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the format of the first number is -- is not in line with our system. So, therefore, we are talking about 1D33-0474. At transcript page 5073, Mr. Tieger advised that he required additional time to review the audio and that he would inform the parties of his position the next day. Now, at that moment, no MFI number was assigned to this audio. Therefore, it slipped through in our later housekeeping sessions where we dealt with MFI lists. I don't think as a matter of fact that Mr. Tieger came back to it. One day has certainly elapsed since transcript page 5073. Could you inform us Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have to speak to Mr. Tieger and get back to the Chamber as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are waiting for your communications. Then the next item is the Albiston report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interim, so we don't lose track of it again, is it possible to MFI -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is a very good suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have to give that suggestion to Mr. Misetic. I'm just his parrot on this message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Misetic develops as a great assistant of the court in slowing down the witnesses, let you wait until the translation is finished, and for me to tell what should be MFI'd. Madam Registrar, the MFI number for 1D33-0474 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D2022, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so no escape possible anymore. The next item, as I said is the Albiston report. There is an issue of the confidential version of the report and the -- the redacted and unredacted version. Now, the unredacted version is in evidence and the redacted version is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It is attached to a motion, Your Honour, so it doesn't have an exhibit number and causes great difficulty in -- in drafting for the final briefs and referencing that material. So we would ask that the redacted version, which we put with our motion, be given an exhibit number. It is uploaded into e-court, and then, for the purposes of final briefs, we have a much more transparent system, because, otherwise, we are referring to vast passages of a confidential document, which, in themselves, do not have confidential passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the Chamber is rather reluctant to have in evidence both redacted and unredacted versions and, of course, the filing of the -- the motion where I think the redacted version is attached to that is public. So reference to the redacted document, I do understand it's primarily a matter of footnotes which would reveal the identity of protected witnesses might serve as well, and that would, as a matter of fact, be our suggestion, that you refer to -- to the report and could be pages, paragraphs, whatever, and that since most of the report in the public version is available to the public, that they would be able -- and as good able to -- to understand your further filings and submissions by looking into this publicly filed redacted version, even if is not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're talking about a very narrow compass here of the Albiston report, in terms of the reason why it was given a confidentiality status. We want to make sure that what we put into our final brief that is uncontroversial is part of a public record, that people can see what we rely upon. We don't want to have vast parts of our final brief redacted for what we can see as being no good reason, which is when -- what would happen with the exhibit being a confidential document. But we -- we're also anxious that our -- Mr. Albiston's report is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I must say that the outcome is the same, whether you -- in a public document, you could only refer to another public document and you suggest that it would be the redacted version which will then be admitted into evidence as a public document. Now, all the references to be made to such a document to be admitted into evidence could be made to the Albiston report as attached to the filing of that date, which would give exactly the same result. The public will understand, and, of course, there's no problem in referring to it, that the unredacted version is in evidence. And if you want to refer to page so-and-so, if there are no redactions, then I do not really see the problem, as long as the reference is always to unredacted portions of the document. But it seems to be a matter of a highly technical nature. You would like to have the Albiston report in the redacted version into evidence, and you see that there are some hesitations to accept both redacted and unredacted versions into evidence. Would it be a suggestion that we try to resolve this matter out of court? It has no substance apart from procedural practicalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then see whether you would still persist in this request or that a solution could be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sure we can find a solution, and it may be it needs explanation on both sides as to what the issues are. I understand the Court's position, and I believe Your Honour would understand the Cermak Defence position, in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that you further discuss the matter primarily with Mr. Nilsson who is the team leader of Chamber support staff for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if it will not be resolved, then, of course, we'll have to find -- then the Chamber, of course, will determine the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, and I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then these were my procedural matters. Is there anything at this moment that should be raised? Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: One minor matter, Your Honours, which is that the 1991 census, the Prosecution, as the Chamber is aware, has uploaded a complete version, and it's at 65 ter 7575, and our suggestion is that that be admitted into evidence, and I know the Chamber expressed some interest in that, and I'd just like to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber has shown an interest to the extent that, sometimes for understanding matters, it's good to know what the composition of the population was, and the Chamber, of course, is fully aware that it considerably changed since that census took place. That is, in various -- I would say various waves, it is has considerably changed. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think at this point we would object to putting it all in, unless we had some understanding of what purposes it would be used for, and so that we don't hear arguments for the first time in final brief. I will note that portions of it related to Sector South have been admitted into evidence as foundation for some of the exhibits we put in. If there is something more specific in relation to other towns that are not yet in evidence, I'm certainly happy to speak to counsel and work something out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- the Chamber had asked it to uploaded into e-court primarily for having an opportunity, if there would be any need to do so, to look into the census. For example when you talked about certain villages as majority Croat or majority Serb, that if there would have been any dispute, that at least we would have the data available. Ms. Gustafson, having heard the concerns expressed by Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can speak to Mr. Misetic about it. One concern we have is that the part that is in evidence is difficult to make out. Maybe we can reach an agreement on just replacing the pages or something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would further discuss that. And if you would please enlarge it as well, so that my eyes are not struggling with what I have seen until now from the 1991 census. What I had forgotten is that I was working from a list dating from yesterday, so, therefore, I would like it finish the items which are on my agenda of today. I would like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now deal with the stipulations to parts of the OTP's pre-trial brief. On the 4th of February, the Gotovina Defence stipulated to paragraphs 105 to 108 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, which relates to armed conflict. An exception was made in relation to the second sentence of paragraph 105. What the Chamber would like to know is whether the Cermak Defence and the Markac Defence would join in these stipulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have, Your Honour, a little bit different approach to that questions. So for the very moment, I have to say that I wouldn't join that stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you partly join that stipulation or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think that path could be most likely, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then please further explore that, that possibility. Of course, from a purely practical point of view, if there's a stipulation by all parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that makes matters more simple. At the same time of course you should not feel to be forced into a stipulation which you do not support. So, therefore, you're invited to see to what extent, if not for the full extent, you can join these stipulations. Perhaps also discuss the matter with other Defence counsel. What caused them to enter into this stipulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it is on the record that the Cermak Defence joins the stipulation, in relation to paragraphs 105 to 108 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, relating to armed conflict, with the exception of the second sentence of paragraph 105. Now, really, the last one on my agenda. In relation to D530 and D424, there were requests for verification of English translations for these exhibits. Internal memos were filed by CLSS in this regard. Have new revised translations been uploaded? I must admit that I do not know which Defence team I should address. I remember that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I saw that you were in a tete-a-tete, as the French say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't follow exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether, upon having received the CLSS memos in relation to D530 and D424, whether the revised translations have been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I can just have a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
